I. 
SUMMARY 
 
Pursuant to 35-A M.R.S. § 307, the Commission rejects Versant Power’s 
(Versant) proposed distribution revenue requirement and instead approves a distribution 
revenue requirement of approximately $169,520,931, which represents an increase in 
rates of approximately $31.9 million (or about 23.2%).1 For Versant’s typical residential 
customer (using 500 kWh per month) this represents an approximately $11.15 increase 
in the customer’s monthly bill. This distribution rate increase will be applied evenly 
across all rate classes and rate elements in both Versant’s Maine Public District and its 
Bangor Hydro District and will take effect on April 1, 2025. 
 
Due to affordability concerns expressed by Versant customers, the Office of the 
Public Advocate, Aroostook Energy Association, the Commission seeks to balance 
minimizing the rate increase resulting from this proceeding with Versant’s need to 
continue to make significant investments in its distribution grid and operations to meet 
customers’ and the grid’s evolving needs.2 As a result of this balancing effort, the 
approved distribution revenue requirement does not fund all of the investments that 
Versant seeks to make at this time.3 However, this decision does not mean that the 
projects or staffing associated with those investments are not worthy of future 
consideration. Rather, the Commission endeavors to approve a pace of investment that 
will be more affordable for Versant’s customers. Because Versant’s approved revenue 
requirement is materially less than what Versant believes is needed at this time, the 
Commission anticipates that Versant will return to the Commission within the next few 
years for a future distribution rate increase. Thus, this rate increase may be viewed as a 
“bridge” to the next distribution rate case. The Commission encourages Versant to, in its 
next distribution rate filing, consider proposing a multi-year alternative rate plan that 
incorporates a well-conceived, detailed, and measured investment and operational plan 
that is designed to achieve Versant’s goals at a measured and relatively affordable

II. 
KEY DRIVERS OF RATE CHANGE 
 
Versant initially requested a rate year revenue requirement of $171,758,379, 
which was an increase of $34,147,335 (24.8%) from rate year revenues at current rates. 
In its rebuttal testimony, Versant increased its request, seeking approval of a rate year 
revenue requirement of $173,754,864 (i.e., an increase of $36,052,541 (26.3%) over 
rate year revenues at current rates). Exhibit Reb-1 Dist. RRM.  
 
Notably, this increase includes about $6.6 million of deferred costs already 
approved by the Commission in other dockets. Those deferred costs include $3.1 
million of deferred amounts from the Company’s last rate case (Docket No. 2022-
00255), $1.7 million of deferred storms costs associated with December 2022 storm 
recovery (Docket No. 2023-00140), and $1.8 million of deferred storm costs associated 
with a September 2023 storm recovery (Docket No. 2024-00046).4  
 
Other than these deferred costs, the largest contributors to the proposed 
increase are (1) incremental investment in plant, (2) increased payroll expenses, (3) 
vegetation management, and (4) inflationary impacts on the company’s operating costs.

IV. 
LEGAL STANDARD 
 
Any rate collected by Versant must be “just and reasonable.” 35-A M.R.S. 
§ 301(2). A main objective in rate-setting is “to achieve a proper balance between the 
right of the utility’s investors to earn a fair return on their investment and the right of 
ratepayers to a fair charge based on the value of the services provided by the utility.” 
New England Tel. & Tel. Co. v. Pub. Utils. Comm’n, 448 A.2d 272, 288 (Me. 1982); Am. 
Ass’n of Retired Persons v. Pub. Utils. Comm’n, 678 A.2d 1025, 1030–31 (Me. 1996). 
 
The Commission’s findings of fact supporting its revenue requirement decision 
must rest on substantial evidence in the evidentiary record. Cent. Me. Power Co. v. Pub. 
Utils. Comm’n, 109 A.2d 512, 513 (Me. 1954) (“[T]he basic question before us is 
whether or not the Commission has fixed reasonable and just rates, supported by 
substantial evidence, which will produce a fair return upon the reasonable value of the 
property of the Company used or required to be used in its service to the public within 
the state.”) The methodology the Commission uses in rate cases “need not be 
suggested by any witness in the record” but instead “lies within the Commission’s 
expertise and discretion and is subject only to a test of reasonableness. If the 
methodology is reasonable, then the result will not be disturbed if the factual findings 
employed in that methodology are supported by the record.” Mars Hill & Blaine Water 
Co. v. Pub. Utils. Comm’n, 397 A.2d 570, 576. (Me. 1979).

A. 
Service Quality Indices (SQIs) 
 
First on the list is Versant’s service quality. The Stipulation in Versant’s last 
distribution rate case, Docket No. 2022-00255, created a Service Quality Index (SQI) 
mechanism with automatic penalties if Versant did not meet the target performance 
levels specified in that stipulation. The SQI mechanism in Docket No. 2022-00255 was 
derived, in part, from an earlier SQI mechanism implemented as a result of the ENMAX 
acquisition case. See generally Versant Power and Maine Electric Power Company, 
Request for Approval of Reorganization with ENMAX, Docket No. 2019-00097. The 
mechanism included the following metrics: System Average Interruption Frequency 
Index (SAIFI), Customer Average Interruption Duration Index (CAIDI), Calls Answered 
within 30 Seconds, Abandoned Calls, Estimated Bills, Bill Errors, and Field Service 
Requests, from 2023 through 2025. Since Versant’s last rate case, the Commission has 
also imposed minimum SQIs on Versant (and Central Maine Power Company), 
pursuant to legislation, through Chapter 320 of the Commission’s rules. See generally 
Maine Public Utilities Commission, Investigation into Utility Service Quality Standards, 
Docket No. 2022-00279. 
 
As discussed below, the Commission approves an SQI mechanism in this case 
to ensure Versant’s customers benefit from Versant’s significant increase in capital 
spending. Alternatively, the Commission considered allowing the current SQI 
mechanism to expire and disallowing a substantial portion of approximately $10.6 
million of Versant’s proposed increases in reliability-related capital investments. 
However, given Versant’s reliability and other service quality needs, the Commission 
concludes that Versant’s customers will benefit from a higher level of funding tied to 
measurable achievement of service quality metrics versus a lower level of funding with 
no additional service measures (beyond the minimum service standards set through 
Chapter 320 of the Commission’s Rules. 
 
1. 
Versant’s Position 
 
Versant’s initial filing in the present case did not include any SQI mechanism. 
Moreover, in its rebuttal, Versant opposed Staff’s SQI proposals in the Bench Analysis 
and did not present any alternative. Versant Reb. Test. of John Flynn at 13-14.  
 
Not until the hearing did Versant’s witness, John Flynn, offer a new position on 
behalf of Versant. During the December 2024 hearing, Versant proposed to adopt 
Staff’s SQI proposal as set forth in the Reply Bench Analysis. However, Versant’s 
position included the following limitations: (1) it only agreed to the implementation of 
these SQIs for 2026, (2) it proposed a limitation on penalties for individual metrics, and 
(3) it altered the calculation of the Bill Error metric to reflect Bill Accuracy instead. ODR-
007-001. Of further note, later in the hearing, Versant was critical of aspects of its 
current SQI mechanism (including storm exclusion and the role of weather variability), 
despite the fact that this mechanism was agreed to by Versant in the stipulation of 
settlement in its last rate case, that a similar mechanism is in effect under Ch. 320 
regardless of the outcome of this rate case, and that Versant witness Flynn had just

4. 
Decision 
 
The Commission approves an SQI mechanism to ensure Versant’s customers 
benefit from its significant increase in capital spending. 
 
As a preliminary matter, the Commission has the legal authority to impose SQIs 
in the context of this rate case. First, the Legislature expressed its desire to measure 
certain categories of transmission and distribution utilities service to customers in 35-A 
M.R.S. § 301(1-A).13 A reasonable corollary to the Commission’s authority to approve or 
disapprove a utility’s distribution revenue requirement is the Commission’s ability to 
measure the effectiveness of the utility’s management of that funding. One methodology 
to measure this is through SQIs. Thus, inherent in the Commission’s responsibility 
under Section 301(2) to establish rates that are just and reasonable is the ability to 
measure the effectiveness of those rates to ensure that, as required by Section 301(1), 
that utilities “furnish safe, reasonable and adequate facilities and service.” Second, the 
Commission possesses broad implied and inherent powers that must be liberally

Here, the need for the Commission to impose SQIs at this juncture is clear. 
Versant’s rate request includes a substantial increase in capital spending designed to 
improve or sustain system reliability. In particular, Versant proposes an increase of 
$10,674,529 in these investments between the test year and the rate year. EXM-003-
010, EXM-003-011, ODR-002-011. This entails a one-year increase of 34.6 percent in 
capital spending on projects to improve or sustain system reliability. In light of these 
requests, the Commission emphasizes that Versant’s customers must receive 
substantial value for an increase in investments that will result in a substantial increase 
in rates and that value must be measurable. 
 
Moreover, Versant’s reluctance to develop meaningful SQIs throughout most of 
this proceeding reveals to the Commission that Versant is not sufficiently motivated to 
improve reliability or being held accountable through a meaningful SQI. The 
Commission also has broader concerns about Versant’s capital planning process, 
including the apparent lack of a comprehensive methodology to prioritize capital 
investments subject to a budget constraint (see Section V.E, infra.) 
 
For these reasons, the Commission approves an SQI mechanism to ensure 
Versant’s customers benefit from its significant increase in capital spending. A summary 
of the SQIs imposed here are as follows: (1) the Commission maintains the SQI 
mechanism currently in effect through 2025 as a result of the Stipulation in Docket No.

reframed positively as a “Bill Accuracy” metric; (3) the Commission adopts Staff’s Reply

a 1% in the CAIDI target through the years 2026 and 2027); and (4) the Commission 
declines to make any further changes to the penalty calculation or storm exclusion

The Commission notes three additional observations regarding Versant’s SQI 
mechanism.  
 
First, the Commission views the Company’s capital investment proposals and 
SQI mechanisms as linked. In an alternative scenario without an SQI mechanism as 
initially proposed by Versant, the Commission may disallow a substantial portion of 
Versant’s proposed increases (approximately $10.6 million) in reliability-related capital 
investment. In that scenario, the minimum service standards under Ch. 320 would 
remain in effect. This scenario resembles Versant’s initial position in this case, albeit 
with a significant reduction in revenue requirement due to the disallowance of 
incremental capital expenditure.

Second, the Commission observes that Versant is critical of its SQI mechanism, 
despite its agreement to that mechanism as part of a settlement in Docket No. 2022-
00255. Moreover, the discussion of the SQI mechanism was substantially delayed in 
this case by Versant’s failure to present an alternative, or any constructive proposals or 
changes, until the day of the hearing. Versant should use the time between the 
conclusion of this rate case and the beginning of its next rate case as an opportunity to 
conduct a thorough re-evaluation of its reliability results, investments, and accountability 
mechanisms. In Versant’s next rate case, the Commission expects that Versant’s initial 
direct testimony will include a meaningful, binding, multi-year SQI mechanism with 
automatic penalties that is paired with well-justified capital investments to improve 
reliability at efficient cost. 
 
Finally, the Commission notes that during the February 11, 2025 oral argument, 
there was discussion of a possible follow-on proceeding to address Versant’s SQIs. 
Versant indicated it was open to such a proceeding, as did the OPA and EMT. However, 
there are a number of other currently pending proceedings that could inform this topic. 
For example, Versant is currently hosting stakeholder meetings as part of its integrated 
grid planning effort (MPUC Docket No. 2022-00322), which could provide an opportunity 
for stakeholders to have such discussions. In addition, there is a pending audit of 
Versant’s management efficiency (MPUC Docket No. 2024-00111), the results of which 
could also inform future SQIs.  
 
On balance, the Commission concludes that the most efficient approach at this 
juncture is to adopt the SQI adjustments described above rather than wait for the results 
of other proceedings or the results of another new proceeding. The evidentiary record in 
this case is sufficiently developed to support the modest SQIs adopted here to be in 
place through 2027. However, this should not dissuade Versant from working with 
stakeholders on a more robust SQI proposal to be considered in its next distribution rate 
case.  
 
B. 
Credit and Collections   
 
Versant’s credit and collections practices impact two aspects of its accounting. 
The first is Versant’s bad debt expense; the second is the amount of Versant’s cash 
working capital. Each category is addressed below. 
 
1. 
Versant’s Initial Proposal 
 
As to bad debt, Versant uses the average of the actual bad debt expense as a 
percentage of revenue to forecast the expected bad debt expense in the rate year. The 
revenue forecast used is the test-year actual revenue plus the incremental distribution 
revenue requested in the filing. The forecasted bad debt expense is compared to the 
test year actual bad debt expense to determine the cost-of-service adjustment after 
adjusting for the amount allocated to transmission. Versant Rev. Req. Test. at 35. 
Versant calculates the projected revenue using the test year revenue increased and 
annualized based upon the proposed rate increase and rate effective date. Versant

2. 
Staff’s Position Regarding Versant’s Credit and Collections 
Practices 
 
Staff expressed serious concern about Versant’s past due accounts receivables, 
pointing out that, over the past ten years, Versant’s bad debt expense ranged from 1% 
to 2% of billed jurisdictional revenues, and over that same period, the dollar amount of 
bad debt expense increased by 65% while the dollar amount of billed jurisdictional 
revenues increased by only 33%.  
 
While this increase warrants attention, Staff was most troubled by a dramatic 
increase in the dollar amount of Versant’s past due accounts receivable. B.A. 30:13–29. 
In particular, Staff was concerned by the increase in the number of days associated with 
the revenue lag—from the 51.01 days used in Docket No. 2017-00198 to the 70.82 
days that Versant proposes in this proceeding. According to Staff, this change was 
primarily due to the increase in the collection lag from 32.29 days to 51.71 days. If the

rate base. Specifically, the return on rate base (and thus revenue requirement) would 
see a $517,258 reduction.16 In its analysis of the root cause of this problem, Staff 
determined that the past due accounts receivable problem appears to begin in 2018.

1. 
AES’s Position48 
 
AEA proposes that the Commission require Versant to reflect unfunded reserves 
within its rate base to “give credit” to customers for customer-funded operating reserves 
held by Versant. AEA defines unfunded reserves as expenses recovered in rates prior to 
the actual expenditure. AEA Brief at 7. For example, AEA opines that the $1.3 million 
that is on Versant’s books for accrued vacation time is an unfunded reserve. AEA also 
notes that vacation expenses for the test year are included in Versant’s proposed 
revenue requirement. It therefore follows, according to AEA, that the average balance of 
the test year’s reserve should also be reflected in rates.   
 
AEA further notes that including unfunded reserves in the rate base aligns with 
established practices for accumulated depreciation and accumulated deferred income 
taxes (ADIT), which are rate base credits that have long been recognized by the 
Commission. According to AEA, both accumulated depreciation and ADIT represent 
reserves on the books where the associated expenses have been funded by customers 
through rate charges. 
 
2. 
Versant’s Position 
 
Versant disagrees with AEA that an unfunded reserve for accrued vacation exists 
or that it should be deducted from rate base. Versant states that beyond Mr. Wilcox’s 
statement that he believes that the expense is recovered in rates in advance of 
payment, no other evidence has been provided by AEA to support this claim. Versant 
argues that if distribution rates were set on a formula rate where actual costs were used 
to set rates on an annual basis with a true-up mechanism, Versant would have collected 
amounts in rates in advance of payment but that is not the case. Distribution rates are 
only set through a rate proceeding. Therefore, it is more likely that the cost of the 
accrued vacation liability was in fact borne by Versant’s shareholders at any particular 
time because the rates are not reset annually and therefore lag its actual costs and also 
because Versant does not include a known and measurable adjustment for vacation 
accruals.  
 
3. 
Decision  
 
The Commission finds that the AEA has not provided sufficient evidence to show 
that an unfunded reserve exists for the accrued vacation liability. Specifically, there is no 
documentation showing the lag between when accrued vacation was funded by 
ratepayers and paid by Versant.
